# Security

Baseline security applies whatever the chosen authentication mode.

Marker after the identifier: a tool name = tooled constraint (the build or the commit fails); `guidance` = rule of conduct checked in review.

## Base rules

### Rules

- **CORE-030** · `gitleaks` — Secrets and environment-specific values come from environment variables; `.env.example` is committed and `.env` is ignored.
  Why: Configuration that differs per environment must never be a code change.
- **CORE-031** · `gitleaks` — No credential, token or private key is ever committed; the gitleaks pre-commit hook blocks the commit.
  Why: A secret in history is compromised even after it is removed.
- **CORE-032** · guidance — The only diagnostic endpoint exposed is `/health`; no endpoint returns configuration, environment or dumps.
  Why: A diagnostics endpoint is a configuration leak waiting for the first scan.
- **CORE-033** · guidance — CORS origins are an explicit list read from configuration; `AllowAnyOrigin` is never used outside `Development`.
  Why: A wildcard origin turns every browser into a client of the API.
- **CORE-034** · guidance — The response security headers set by the pipeline (`X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, HSTS) are never removed without an ADR.
  Why: ASP.NET Core does not set them by default; the skeleton adds them and each one closes a class of browser attacks for free.
- **CORE-035** · `nuget-audit` — A package with a known vulnerability fails the build, NuGet audit warnings being treated as errors.
  Why: Most breaches exploit a known, already patched vulnerability.
- **CORE-036** · guidance — Detailed error pages are enabled in `Development` only; every other environment answers with `ProblemDetails`.
  Why: A stack trace hands an attacker the framework versions and the internal file layout.

### Anti-patterns

- **CORE-AP-030** · `gitleaks` — A password or API key written in `appsettings.json`.
  Why: The value is committed, shared and impossible to rotate per environment.
  Instead: An environment variable read by the configuration, documented in `.env.example`.
- **CORE-AP-031** · guidance — `app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage()` left outside the `Development` branch to "help debugging in staging".
  Why: Staging is reachable and the page prints the exception, the source and the configuration.
  Instead: Read the logs, which carry the same information without publishing it.
- **CORE-AP-032** · guidance — `AllowAnyOrigin().AllowAnyHeader().AllowAnyMethod()` to make a local front end work.
  Why: The shortcut ships to production because nobody remembers it.
  Instead: The local origin in the `Development` configuration and the real one in production.

### Expected environment variables

| Variable | Example | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `JWT_AUTHORITY` | `https://auth.example.com/realms/app` | OIDC provider that issues the tokens; the application refuses to start without it. |
| `JWT_AUDIENCE` | `` | Expected audience of the tokens; empty disables the audience check (SECJ-004). |

## Option `security-jwt-bearer`

Stateless API validating JWT access tokens issued by an external OIDC provider.

### Rules

- **SECJ-001** · guidance — Every endpoint requires an authenticated user by default; making one public is an explicit `[AllowAnonymous]`.
  Why: A forgotten attribute must fail closed, not open.
- **SECJ-002** · `gitleaks` — The application validates tokens and never issues any; it holds no signing key and no client secret.
  Why: Issuing tokens is the identity provider's job; a key held here is a key to steal.
- **SECJ-003** · guidance — The authority comes from `JWT_AUTHORITY` and the audience from `JWT_AUDIENCE`; neither is hard-coded.
  Why: The same build must run against the test and the production provider.
- **SECJ-004** · guidance — Issuer, audience, signature and lifetime are all validated; disabling one of them requires an ADR.
  Why: Each check dropped turns a token from another system into a valid one here.
- **SECJ-005** · `arch-test` — Business tests run with `Security:Enabled=false`; authentication itself has its own test.
  Why: A business test must not depend on an identity provider being reachable.
- **SECJ-006** · guidance — Authorities come from the token claims; no role is stored per user in the application.
  Why: Roles kept in the identity provider stay consistent across every service that trusts it.

### Anti-patterns

- **SECJ-AP-001** · guidance — Decoding the JWT by hand in a middleware to "read the user".
  Why: Signature, expiry and issuer checks end up skipped one by one.
  Instead: Read `User.Claims`, which the handler has already validated.
- **SECJ-AP-002** · guidance — `RequireHttpsMetadata = false` to make a local provider work.
  Why: The metadata, hence the signing keys, then travel in clear text.
  Instead: Keep it enabled outside `Development`, where the skeleton already relaxes it.
